paragraphs.heading: Mixing solutions
paragraphs.text: Quantum superposition is a basic rule of quantum mechanics: if two states each solve the Schrödinger equation, any linear combination of them solves it as well. This holds because the Schrödinger equation is linear in time and position. Put more exactly, a system's state is built by combining all the eigenfunctions of the Schrödinger equation that governs that system.

paragraphs.heading: Adding waves together
paragraphs.text: The theory assumes that a wave equation fully describes the state of a quantum system at every moment. It also requires that equation to be linear and homogeneous. Together these mean that if Ψ₁ and Ψ₂ are both solutions, then so is Ψ = c₁Ψ₁ + c₂Ψ₂, whatever complex numbers c₁ and c₂ you pick. With more than two solutions, any combination of all of them is again a solution.

paragraphs.heading: What a measurement shows
paragraphs.text: Picture two states, A and B. Some observation is certain to give result a when the system is in A, and certain to give a different result b when it is in B. Make the observation on a superposition of A and B and you get sometimes a, sometimes b, never anything else. How often each turns up depends on how heavily A and B are weighted in the mix. So the mixed state is in between only in its probabilities, not in the results you actually see.

paragraphs.heading: The qubit
paragraphs.text: In a quantum computer, the qubit stands in for an ordinary bit, but instead of holding one of two values it is a superposition of both. Its state is written as two weights, c₀ and c₁, called probability amplitudes, both complex numbers, attached to the states |0⟩ and |1⟩, which match the classical 0 and 1. A measurement finds |0⟩ with probability |c₀|² and |1⟩ with probability |c₁|². Until the measurement, the qubit is in a superposition of both. Controlling this is a central challenge: the superposition must survive unwanted interactions, yet computing needs interactions.

paragraphs.heading: Interference and path knowledge
paragraphs.text: The interference fringes of the double-slit experiment are another example of superposition at work. Adding amplitudes this way only works if there is no way, even in principle, to know which path the particle took. Nobody has to actually look. If the path information can be reached in principle, even when it has spread into the environment beyond any hope of recovery, the interference pattern is destroyed.

paragraphs.heading: Schrödinger's cat
paragraphs.text: Erwin Schrödinger imagined a cat shut in a steel chamber with a radioactive source that could release poison gas. He proposed it be described as a superposition of two states, a living cat and a cat killed by the poison. He meant this to show how outlandish superposition becomes when used carelessly. Other analyses keep only the microscopic parts, the radioactive source and its detector, in superposed states.

paragraphs.heading: Ever larger objects
paragraphs.text: Superposition has now been shown for objects that are large by quantum standards. Double-slit experiments have been run with buckyballs and with oligoporphyrin molecules of up to 2000 atoms. Metal clusters with more than 7,000 atoms have also been put in superposition. A piezoelectric tuning fork made of about 10 trillion atoms has been placed in a superposition of vibrating and not vibrating.
